title: Facing Islamophobia
hook: A stare, a comment, a headline thrown at you. How to stay safe, keep your dignity, and know you're not alone.

screens.text: Sooner or later, many Muslims meet it: a rude comment, a "joke" at work, someone yelling from a car. If it's happened to you, it wasn't your fault. Today: how to stay safe, keep your dignity, and get support.
**It's real, and it isn't about you.** Fear of Muslims mostly grows where people have never actually met one [Field Guide ch. 16]. That doesn't make it okay, and you don't have to fix it alone.
bubbles: Two priorities, in this order: **your safety first**, then **your dignity**.

steps.text: If you feel unsafe, don't argue
Move toward other people or a staffed place
Afterwards, write down what happened: time, place, what was said, and photos if it's safe
Report it to the police and to **CAIR** (the Council on American-Islamic Relations) at cair.com/report
Tell {{mentor.name}} too. You don't carry it alone

screens.situation: Aaliyah is loading groceries when a man in the parking lot starts shouting at her about Muslims and walks toward her.

options.text: Get in the car, lock it, drive somewhere with people, and call 911 if he follows. Later, write it down and report it to CAIR
options.feedback: Yes. Safety first. Leaving isn't weakness. Writing it down and reporting helps you and others.

options.text: Stand her ground and argue back so he learns he's wrong
options.feedback: Understandable, but risky. Someone shouting isn't open to learning. Get safe first; dignity can wait a minute.

options.text: Shrug it off and tell nobody, since nothing physical happened
options.feedback: Not quite. Threats still count. Reporting to CAIR and telling your mentor means you don't carry it alone.

screens.text: **Then, dignity.** The Qur'an describes Allah's servants as people who walk gently, and answer the ignorant with "peace" [Q 25:63]. It also says: push back bad with what is better, and an enemy may become a close friend [Q 41:34].
bubbles: When some men insulted the Prophet ﷺ, 'Aisha snapped back at them. He told her that Allah loves gentleness in every matter [Bukhari 6024].

Not quite. They answer with peace [Q 25:63]. You don't owe anyone an argument.

cards.front: A hateful comment under your post
cards.back: Don't feed it. Block, report, move on. You don't owe a troll a debate.
A calm line works: "That's not funny to me. I'd rather you didn't joke about that." If it continues, write it down and talk to HR.

cards.front: Treated differently at work for being Muslim
cards.back: Keep notes and dates, raise it in writing, and contact CAIR. You have rights, and they can explain them.
That's a chance, not an attack. A short, kind answer can change how someone sees Muslims.

screens.text: **At school.** If you're a teen and get called names, hear "terrorist" jokes, or a teacher says something that feels targeted, you don't have to handle it alone. Tell a teacher, a counselor or a parent you trust, and {{mentor.name}}.
bubbles: Schools are supposed to take harassment seriously, and CAIR helps students too.
If your family doesn't know you're Muslim yet, start with your mentor or a school counselor.

screens.character: Chris, a coworker in his forties. Friendly enough, watches a lot of cable news, and just found out you're Muslim.
screens.setup: At the coffee machine, Chris says: "No offense, but I keep seeing stuff on the news. Isn't Islam kind of a violent religion?"
screens.goal: Answer calmly and briefly, without getting defensive or attacking him. Share one or two true things and leave the door open.
screens.success_looks_like: The convert stays calm; says something like 'I get why the news makes it look that way'; explains that Islam forbids harming innocent people and that most Muslims are ordinary neighbors; mentions their own experience; maybe offers to answer more questions later. No insults, no lecture.
screens.coach_notes: Chris isn't hostile, just repeating headlines. He pushes once or twice ('But what about the terrorists?'), then softens if the convert stays calm. If the convert gets angry, Chris gets defensive (never abusive). Debrief: praise calm tone and personal examples; suggest a short line if they rambled. If the convert says they've faced real harassment, step out of the role-play and follow the safety rule. No political opinions.

chips: What should I do if I'm harassed for being Muslim?

steps: Save CAIR's report link (cair.com/report) in your phone, next to 911

screens.optional_extra: Think of one calm sentence you could say if someone asks you a hostile question about Islam. Practice it once out loud.

screens.text: Safety first, then dignity. Answer the ignorant with peace, and never carry it alone: tell your mentor and report it to CAIR.
Every calm, kind Muslim someone meets makes the next one's day a little easier. You're one of them now.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Safety comes before any response: leave, go toward people, call 911 in danger; then document (time, place, words, photos if safe) and report to police and CAIR (cair.com/report; CAIR's civil rights line 202-742-6420). Tell the mentor.
- Dignity: Allah's servants answer the ignorant with peace [Q 25:63]; repel bad with what is better [Q 41:34]. When 'Aisha answered insults harshly, the Prophet ﷺ told her Allah loves gentleness in all matters [Bukhari 6024].
- Islamophobia often grows where people don't know Muslims; good character and calm answers help, but the target is never to blame [Field Guide ch. 16].
- At work: document, raise it in writing, contact CAIR. At school (teens): tell a trusted adult (teacher, counselor, parent) and the mentor; CAIR also helps students.

**Likely questions**
- *"I was harassed / attacked."* If it's happening now or they're in danger: safety rule (911, crisis resources). Otherwise: are you safe now? Document, report to police and CAIR, tell your mentor. Offer care first, steps second.
- *"How do I answer 'Isn't Islam violent?'"* Calm and short: Islam forbids harming innocent people; the overwhelming majority of Muslims are ordinary neighbors; offer a personal example. Offer a role-play.
- *"Should I stop wearing hijab / hide that I'm Muslim to stay safe?"* Acknowledge the fear. Don't rule; personal safety decisions and hijab questions go to the imam or a female mentor (Q8).
- *"Do I have to tell people I'm Muslim?"* No. They choose who knows (Spec §3, §6.4).
- *"Someone at school bullies me."* Tell a trusted adult and the mentor; if the family doesn't know they're Muslim, start with the mentor or a counselor.

**Escalate:** any ongoing threat or violence (safety rule, never only the imam queue); workplace discrimination needing legal help (CAIR); a teen being bullied whose parents don't know they're Muslim (mentor).

**Don't**
- Don't give legal advice beyond "contact CAIR or a lawyer."
- Don't encourage confronting a threatening person, retaliating, or posting about an incident in a way that puts the convert at risk.
- No political opinions, no blaming any group, no insults toward people of other faiths.
- Don't imply the convert caused it by how they looked or acted.

**Role-play brief:** Chris is curious, a bit suspicious, never abusive. He repeats headlines and softens when met with calm. Debrief on tone, brevity and one personal example. Safety rule overrides the role-play.
